staircase decorating ideas.bodyHtml:
Staircase decorating ideas can completely transform one of the most overlooked spaces in your home — and when you get it right, your staircase becomes one of the first things guests notice and compliment. Whether you have a sweeping open staircase, a narrow enclosed stairwell, or a compact stairs-and-landing combo, there are clever, stylish ways to make it sing. In this guide, I'm sharing everything I know from over a decade of helping clients style their staircases — from gallery wall layouts and lighting tricks to paint pairings and common mistakes to sidestep.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever walked past your staircase a hundred times a week without really looking at it — and then one day thought, "why does this space feel so blank and sad"? I've heard that from so many clients. The staircase is genuinely one of the most used areas of any home, and yet it's one of the last places people think to decorate. If you've been putting off sorting yours, maybe because it feels awkward or you're not sure where to start, you're in exactly the right place. A well-chosen piece of wall art alone can make the entire space feel intentional, finished, and genuinely impressive.

Quick answer: The best staircase decorating ideas combine wall art or a gallery wall, thoughtful lighting, and a cohesive colour scheme to turn wasted vertical space into a visual feature. Focus on scale — staircases often need larger or more numerous pieces than you'd expect — and always account for the angle of the wall when hanging art.

A staircase isn't just a functional route between floors. It's a vertical gallery, a transitional space with more wall square footage than most people realise, and an opportunity to show off real personality. When I talk about staircase decorating, I mean everything from what goes on the walls (art, mirrors, shelves, lighting) to the balustrade, the treads themselves, and how colour and texture play together across the whole area. If you're looking for unique wall art or unique home decor that works specifically in staircase spaces, I'll be pointing you in the right direction throughout this guide.

Types of Staircase Decorating Ideas by Style: Modern, Traditional, and Rustic

The first thing I always ask a client is: what style is the rest of your home? Because whatever you do on the staircase, it needs to feel like it belongs to the same house. The good news is that every main decorating style — modern, traditional, and rustic — has a genuinely brilliant set of staircase ideas to draw from.

For a modern staircase, think clean lines, a limited colour palette (often white, black, grey, or warm neutrals), and statement art in simple frames or even unframed canvas. Floating shelves with sculptural objects, minimalist metal railings, and sleek pendant lighting all keep the space looking sharp and uncluttered.

A traditional staircase suits a more layered approach: stair runners in rich patterns, ornate balustrades, framed oil-style prints or botanical illustrations, and wall panelling with classic moulding. It's a style that rewards going a little bolder — deeper colours on the walls and heavier frames work brilliantly here.

Rustic staircases are my personal favourite to style. Think exposed wood banisters, distressed metal fixtures, woven wall hangings, and earthy tones. Mixing textures — rough linen, hammered iron, reclaimed timber — gives rustic staircases enormous warmth without any effort at all.

Quick Style Reference Guide

  • Modern: White or greige walls, unframed canvas or thin black frames, minimalist shelving, statement pendants
  • Traditional: Wall panelling, gallery frames in gold or dark wood, stair runners, botanical or portrait prints
  • Rustic: Exposed wood, macramé hangings, woven baskets on hooks, earthy terracotta tones, plants
  • Scandi/Japandi: Pale oak, pared-back prints, low-hung sconces, natural materials only
  • Industrial: Exposed brick, metal railings, monochrome photography, Edison-bulb pendants
Pro Tip: Before buying anything, hold paint swatches and art print samples against your staircase wall in both daytime and evening light. Stairwells can be much darker than you expect, and what looks perfect in a shop can look flat or dingy on the wall.

Wall Art and Gallery Wall Ideas for Staircases

A gallery wall on a staircase is one of those things that looks effortless when it's done well — but takes a bit of thought to get right. The key difference from a flat living room wall is that you're working with a diagonal space, so the composition needs to follow the angle of the stairs rather than sit as a neat horizontal block.

The most popular approach is what I call the "staircase stagger": a row of frames that steps upward with each tread, maintaining equal spacing between each piece. It reads as one unified display, but each frame sits at a different height. This works brilliantly with a mix of sizes — say, two or three larger anchor pieces surrounded by smaller prints and photographs.

I had a client in a Victorian terraced house in Bristol — she had a narrow staircase with high ceilings, and she'd bought about twelve small frames in different sizes but couldn't work out how to arrange them. We laid them out on the floor first (always do this), photographed it, then transferred the arrangement to the wall using paper templates before putting a single nail in. The result was stunning and took the guesswork out completely.

Gallery Wall Layout Options for Staircases

  • The Diagonal Stagger: Frames step upward in a diagonal line following the stair angle — the most classic choice
  • The Clustered Grid: A tight block of same-sized frames in a grid, works best on a landing or flat wall above stairs
  • The Eclectic Mix: Different sizes, frames, and even objects (mirrors, small shelves) arranged loosely — needs a consistent colour palette to hold it together
  • The Mono Gallery: All black-and-white photography in matching black frames — graphic, modern, and impossible to get wrong

Pro Tip: Use paper templates (cut to frame size) and low-tack masking tape to plan your gallery wall layout before you commit to any nails. Take a photo of the template arrangement on the wall — it's much easier to tweak on your phone than in real life.

How to Hang Art in a Stairwell — Step by Step

Knowing how to hang art in a stairwell is one of the most searched questions I come across, and honestly, it trips people up not because it's technically difficult, but because the angled wall messes with your spatial judgement. What looks level to your eye usually isn't, because the stairs themselves are on a slope.

The golden rule: hang art relative to the wall, not the floor. Use a spirit level every single time, and don't trust your eye alone in a stairwell — the angle of the stairs will fool you into hanging everything crooked.

When it comes to height, the standard guidance is to hang the centre of each artwork at roughly 145–150cm from the floor directly below that piece. In a stairwell, "the floor below" means the nearest tread, not the bottom of the stairs. This keeps everything proportional as you move up.

Step-by-Step Guide to Hanging Stairwell Art

  • Step 1: Decide on your layout. Lay all frames on the floor first and photograph your preferred arrangement.
  • Step 2: Cut paper templates the same size as each frame and tape them to the wall with low-tack tape.
  • Step 3: Step back (literally — go to the top or bottom of the stairs) and check the spacing looks even from a distance.
  • Step 4: Mark nail positions through each paper template using a pencil. Use a spirit level for every mark.
  • Step 5: Remove templates and hang the frames. Use picture hooks rated for the weight of each piece.
  • Step 6: Walk up and down the stairs slowly and check that nothing looks off from eye level in motion — this is the final test.
Pro Tip: On plasterboard staircase walls, always use wall anchors or find the stud when hanging heavier frames. Stairwells are high-traffic vibration zones — you don't want anything working loose over time.

How to Decorate a High Stairwell Wall

A high stairwell wall is simultaneously the most exciting and most intimidating canvas in any home. The sheer scale of it means that small art looks completely lost — and yet many people default to hanging a few small frames and wondering why the space still looks bare.

The honest answer to how to decorate a high stairwell wall is: go bigger than you think you need to. A single oversized print or canvas (think 100cm wide and taller) anchors the wall properly. Alternatively, a floor-to-ceiling arrangement of framed pieces — scaled up and spaced generously — works as a dramatic statement.

One approach I love for really tall stairwells is treating the wall like a mural backdrop. Large-format photographic prints, oversized botanical illustrations, or even peel-and-stick wallpaper murals can fill a tall stairwell beautifully without requiring scaffolding to hang.

Ideas for Tall Stairwell Walls

  • One oversized canvas or print as a single anchor statement
  • A floor-to-ceiling gallery arrangement with varied frame sizes
  • A large wallpaper mural panel behind the stair run
  • Oversized mirrors to bounce light and add depth
  • Wall-mounted sconces at two or three heights to draw the eye upward
  • Hanging macramé or textile art that fills vertical space naturally

Real Example: I worked with a family in a 1930s semi-detached who had a stunning tall stairwell but had covered it with eight tiny prints in mismatched frames. We replaced everything with two large-format prints and a single oversized mirror — the space looked three times the size within an afternoon.

How to Decorate an Enclosed Stairwell

Enclosed stairwells — the kind with walls on both sides and often no natural light — are tricky, but they're not hopeless. In fact, the enclosed nature of the space actually works in your favour: it creates a contained, immersive atmosphere that you can really lean into.

When I think about how to decorate an enclosed stairwell, the first thing I address is light. Without natural light, the space will feel oppressive unless you add artificial light at multiple points — wall-mounted sconces, LED strip lighting under handrails, or even a pendant that drops down the stairwell from above.

For enclosed staircase wall decorating ideas, light-reflective choices are your friends: pale paint colours, mirrors, metallic-framed art, and high-gloss or satin finishes on woodwork. I'd also suggest keeping the wall decor on one side only if the stairwell is narrow — both sides decorated in a tight space can feel claustrophobic.

Enclosed Stairwell Decor Checklist

  • Add wall-mounted sconces for warm, layered lighting
  • Use light paint colours — off-white, pale stone, or soft sage
  • Hang at least one mirror to maximise the sense of space
  • Keep wall decor on one wall only if the stairwell is under 90cm wide
  • Use a stair runner to add warmth underfoot without cluttering the walls
  • Add a single trailing plant on the landing above to draw the eye upward
Pro Tip: In an enclosed stairwell, a large mirror placed opposite the main light source will effectively double the perceived width of the space. This is the single quickest fix I know for a dark, cramped stairwell.

Staircase Railing and Balustrade Decorating Options

The railing and balustrade are structural elements, yes — but they're also a huge part of the visual character of your staircase. Updating them (or simply dressing them up) can make a bigger difference than anything you put on the walls.

If you have an older staircase with traditional timber spindles, painting them is one of the most cost-effective transformations available. Classic white or off-white spindles against a dark handrail looks crisp and timeless. For a more modern feel, painting spindles in a deep charcoal, navy, or even black gives a dramatic, high-end look at almost no cost.

Beyond paint, you can wrap newel posts in rope or leather for a nautical or rustic feel, add woven garlands for seasonal or permanent decorative interest, or swap outdated spindles for sleek glass panels or steel rods if your budget allows for a full update.

Pro Tip: Before you decide on new spindles or panels, check with a structural engineer or joiner that your existing newel posts can support the fixings. It's a quick check that saves expensive surprises later.

Lighting Ideas to Enhance Staircase Decor

Lighting is the most underused tool in staircase decorating — full stop. I genuinely believe you can have the most beautiful gallery wall in the world, but if your staircase is lit by a single harsh ceiling bulb, it will never look as good as it should.

The key principle is layered lighting. You want at least two sources in a staircase: ambient light (overall brightness for safety) and accent or decorative lighting that adds atmosphere. Wall-mounted sconces are the most popular choice because they sit at eye level, cast a warm glow, and add visual interest to the wall even when switched off.

LED strip lighting under the handrail or beneath each tread is a modern touch that looks brilliant at night and significantly improves stair safety. For tall stairwells, a pendant that drops down through the full height of the stairwell can be an extraordinary focal point — think an oversized drum shade or a sculptural cage pendant.

Staircase Lighting Options

  • Wall sconces: Best for adding warmth and visual interest at eye level
  • Under-tread LED strips: Modern, dramatic, and brilliant for safety
  • Pendant lights: Ideal for tall stairwells; choose scale carefully
  • Recessed ceiling spotlights: Clean and minimal; aim down the staircase run, not flat
  • Lantern-style pendants: Great for traditional or rustic staircases
  • Picture lights over key art pieces: For gallery walls — adds drama and draws the eye

Pro Tip: Warm white bulbs (2700K–3000K) always look better in stairwells than cool white. Cool light makes the space feel clinical and tends to flatten wall colours — warm light makes everything feel considered and welcoming.

Colour Scheme and Paint Ideas Paired with Wall Decor

Choosing a colour scheme for your staircase is a bit different from choosing one for a room, because your staircase is usually a transitional space connecting different areas of the house. The colours need to feel cohesive with both your hallway and your upper landing — not just pretty in isolation.

My go-to approach is to pick one colour from your hall or landing and use the staircase as the place where you deepen or accent it. So if your hall is pale stone, your staircase wall might go in a warm taupe or even a deep heritage green — it creates a sense of progression as you move through the house.

Is painting your stairs a good idea? Absolutely, yes — painted stair risers (the vertical front face of each step) are one of the best budget updates you can do. Plain white risers make everything look cleaner and bigger, while painted risers in a contrasting colour add a playful, design-forward touch. Just make sure you use a durable floor or stair-specific paint and add a protective varnish over the top.

Staircase Colour Pairing Ideas

  • Pale stone + white woodwork: Safe, timeless, works in any home
  • Deep sage green + natural oak: Warm, organic, brilliant for Scandi or rustic styles

  • Blush pink + warm grey: Soft, modern, brilliant for a contemporary terraced house
  • Warm white + painted risers in a contrasting accent: Budget-friendly with big impact
Pro Tip: Always paint the staircase and landing the same colour on the ceiling and upper wall surfaces — it creates a visual flow that makes the space feel intentionally designed rather than just "decorated in sections".

Small vs Large Staircase Decorating Considerations

Not all staircases are created equal, and the approach that works for a dramatic Victorian double-height stairwell will feel completely wrong in a compact new-build. Getting the scale right is honestly the most important factor in staircase decorating.

In a small staircase, the biggest mistake people make is going too small with their art — using tiny frames that disappear against the wall. Counterintuitively, one medium-to-large print often looks better than five small ones in a tight space. It gives the eye somewhere clear to land without cluttering an already compact area.

In a large staircase, the challenge is filling the space without it feeling wallpapered or frantic. Breathing room between pieces matters. I always recommend that the gaps between frames should be at least as wide as the frame itself — this keeps the display feeling curated rather than crowded.

Factor Small Staircase Large Staircase

Pro Tip: In a small staircase, choose frames with thin profiles (under 2cm wide) or go frameless. Heavy ornate frames make a small wall feel even smaller and can make the staircase feel cramped.

Shoppable Wall Art Recommendations Specific to Staircase Proportions

One of the gaps I notice in most staircase decorating guides is that they show you lovely inspiration images but never tell you what to actually buy. So here's my practical breakdown of the types of wall art that work best for staircase proportions — and why.

For a tall stairwell, you want prints or canvases in portrait orientation — taller than they are wide — which naturally echo the upward movement of the stairs. Abstract line art, tall botanical prints, and architectural photography in portrait format all look exceptional.

For a gallery wall arrangement stepping up with the stairs, mixing landscape and portrait prints in cohesive tones (black and white, or a limited earthy palette) gives the display visual rhythm without chaos. Matching frame colours — all black, all white, or all natural wood — ties mismatched print styles together instantly.

Wall Art Types for Staircase Proportions

  • Tall portrait prints (60x90cm or larger): Perfect for tall stairwells, echoes the upward movement
  • Square prints (50x50cm or 60x60cm): Great for creating uniform grid arrangements on a landing wall
  • Panoramic/wide landscape prints: Works well above a half-landing or on a large flat wall at the top of stairs
  • Abstract line art: Versatile, pairs with any interior style, never dates
  • Botanical or nature prints: Add organic warmth — particularly good in rustic or Scandi staircases
  • Black and white photography: Timeless and cohesive — the safest gallery wall choice

Pro Tip: When buying art for a staircase gallery, order all your prints at the same time and frame them before you hang anything. Seeing all the pieces together in your hand, in their frames, before anything goes on the wall, prevents the most common mistake: a mix of tones and depths that doesn't hang together.

Budget-Friendly vs Luxury Staircase Decorating Ideas

I work with clients at every budget level, and I genuinely believe you can achieve a beautiful staircase without spending a fortune — but you do need to be strategic about where you spend and where you save. The worst approach is to splash out on lots of small things that don't add up to anything cohesive.

At the budget end, painting is always your biggest bang for your buck. A fresh coat on the walls and woodwork, painted stair risers, and a printed geometric stair runner transforms a staircase for a fraction of the cost of a renovation. Add a couple of well-chosen prints in simple frames and a mirror, and you're done.

At the luxury end, the staircase is where bespoke really pays off. Custom joinery for the balustrade, a hand-tufted stair runner, original artwork or photography, and designer pendant lighting create a space that's genuinely one of a kind.

When clients ask how to modernise a staircase on a budget, my honest answer is always: start with paint, add one statement mirror, and choose two or three quality prints in matching frames. That combination alone will transform almost any staircase without you spending more than a couple of hundred pounds.

Pro Tip: Quality frames make budget prints look expensive. A simple print in a thick-profile black or natural oak frame looks like a deliberate, considered choice. The same print in a flimsy thin frame looks like an afterthought.

Common Staircase Decorating Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

After more than a decade of staircase consultations, I could write an entire book on the mistakes I see repeatedly. But I'll give you the most important ones here, because avoiding them is genuinely more valuable than any inspiration board.

The number one mistake is hanging art too low. People instinctively hang things at room-height — around 145cm from the floor — but on a staircase, that often means art ends up at knee level as you walk up. Always hang relative to the wall, following the stair angle, and aim to have the centre of each piece at eye level as you pass it on the stairs, not from the bottom of the staircase.

The second biggest mistake is a mismatch of frame styles with no unifying element. I visited a home where the client had bought frames over several years — gold, silver, black, white, and ornate wooden — all on the same wall. No single piece looked wrong individually, but together it was visual chaos. Picking one frame finish for a gallery wall is the single easiest fix.

What should not be done on a staircase? Cluttering the floor or treads with decorative objects. It's a safety hazard and it makes even a beautifully decorated staircase look messy. Keep the floor of your stairs completely clear — the walls and railing are where the decor lives.

Top Staircase Decorating Mistakes to Avoid

  • Hanging art too low — always follow the stair angle and eye-level rule
  • Mixing too many frame finishes with no unifying element
  • Placing objects on stair treads — a safety risk and a styling mistake
  • Choosing art that is too small for the wall — go bigger than you think
  • Ignoring lighting — a beautiful gallery wall in bad light always disappoints
  • Using too many colours in art and decor — a cohesive palette is key
  • Forgetting to account for the visual experience from both directions (going up and coming down)
Real Example: A client once showed me a staircase she'd decorated herself — lovely prints, good frames — but everything was hung in a perfectly level horizontal row. On a staircase, that horizontal line fought against the diagonal of the stairs and the whole display looked oddly tilted. We re-hung everything following the stair angle in an afternoon and the difference was immediate.

Staircase Wall Decor Ideas: Modern Takes Worth Trying

When I think about staircase wall decor ideas for a modern home, I immediately think about what the latest staircase trends are pointing toward — and right now, it's a move away from fussy gallery walls toward bolder, more intentional statements.

Modern stairwell wall art ideas tend to feature large-scale abstract art, oversized monochrome photography, or even a single dramatic sculptural piece rather than a collection. The idea is "less, but better" — fewer pieces, more considered, with generous space around each one.

Staircase wall decor ideas in a modern style also include architectural elements: wall panelling in a modern reeded or fluted profile, polished plaster finishes, or a graphic accent wall in a single bold colour. These work beautifully as a backdrop to a single piece of statement art or a large mirror.

Modern Staircase Wall Ideas to Try Now

  • One oversized abstract or monochrome print as the sole wall feature
  • Reeded or fluted MDF wall panelling for an architectural texture
  • Polished plaster in a warm tone — zero art needed, the wall is the feature
  • A large round mirror as a dramatic single accent
  • Wall-mounted sculptural lighting that doubles as an art piece
  • A single oversized macramé or woven textile piece for Boho-modern style
[[PRODUCT|oversized abstract canvas wall art for modern staircase]]
Pro Tip: Modern staircase wall decor works best when you commit to restraint. If you're tempted to add "just one more thing", that is usually a sign to stop. The space between pieces is as important as the pieces themselves.

Staircase Decor Styles Worth Exploring

I find that staircase decorating trends evolve more slowly than other rooms — which is actually a good thing. You're making decisions that live with you for years, so it's worth looking at what genuinely suits your house rather than chasing trends. That said, here are the styles I'm most excited about right now that I think have genuine staying power.

The warm Japandi look — a blend of Japanese minimalism and Scandinavian cosiness — is producing some of the most beautiful staircase interiors I've seen. Pale oak treads, warm white walls, a single trailing plant, a ceramic vase on a floating shelf, and no art at all — just clean, calm intention.

At the opposite end, maximalist gallery walls are having a real moment in period homes. Floor-to-ceiling art arrangements in ornate frames, mixed with mirrors and decorative plates, feel genuinely theatrical and exciting. If your home has the bones for it, lean in.

More About Staircase Decorating — Expert Guidance Worth Reading

Getting the most from your staircase starts with understanding the space as a whole rather than decorating it in isolated elements.

The best staircase decorating is always joined up: the colour on the walls, the finish on the balustrade, the choice of lighting, and the art all work together as one composition. For a broader look at the full range of stair decorating possibilities — from open-riser treads to under-stair storage and mural-scale wallpaper — I always recommend reading around the topic. What I'd add from my own experience is this: the staircase is worth investing in both time and thought, because it's genuinely one of the most used spaces in any home. You pass through it multiple times a day, every day. When it looks and feels right, it lifts your mood every single time you use it — and that's not a small thing.

Ready to Transform Your Staircase? Here's Where to Start

If you've made it this far, you're probably already picturing what your staircase could look like — and that's the most important first step. The best thing about staircase decorating is that it doesn't need to happen all at once. Start with one decision: a colour, a piece of art, or a lighting upgrade. Build from there.

Whatever your budget, your style, or the size of your staircase, the core idea is the same: treat it as a real room rather than a corridor you happen to have to walk through. It deserves the same thought and care as any other space in your home — probably more, given how often you're in it.

And honestly? The staircase is often the space that surprises people most once they finally give it attention. Clients who were dreading the project almost always end up saying it became their favourite part of the house.

Staircase decorating ideas can completely transform one of the most overlooked spaces in your home — and when you get it right, your staircase becomes one of the first things guests notice and compliment. Whether you have a sweeping open staircase, a narrow enclosed stairwell, or a compact stairs-and-landing combo, there are clever, stylish ways to make it sing. In this guide, I'm sharing everything I know from over a decade of helping clients style their staircases — from gallery wall layouts and lighting tricks to paint pairings and common mistakes to sidestep.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever walked past your staircase a hundred times a week without really looking at it — and then one day thought, "why does this space feel so blank and sad"? I've heard that from so many clients. The staircase is genuinely one of the most used areas of any home, and yet it's one of the last places people think to decorate. If you've been putting off sorting yours, maybe because it feels awkward or you're not sure where to start, you're in exactly the right place. A well-chosen piece of wall art alone can make the entire space feel intentional, finished, and genuinely impressive.

Quick answer: The best staircase decorating ideas combine wall art or a gallery wall, thoughtful lighting, and a cohesive colour scheme to turn wasted vertical space into a visual feature. Focus on scale — staircases often need larger or more numerous pieces than you'd expect — and always account for the angle of the wall when hanging art.

A staircase isn't just a functional route between floors. It's a vertical gallery, a transitional space with more wall square footage than most people realise, and an opportunity to show off real personality. When I talk about staircase decorating, I mean everything from what goes on the walls (art, mirrors, shelves, lighting) to the balustrade, the treads themselves, and how colour and texture play together across the whole area. If you're looking for unique wall art or unique home decor that works specifically in staircase spaces, I'll be pointing you in the right direction throughout this guide.

Types of Staircase Decorating Ideas by Style: Modern, Traditional, and Rustic

The first thing I always ask a client is: what style is the rest of your home? Because whatever you do on the staircase, it needs to feel like it belongs to the same house. The good news is that every main decorating style — modern, traditional, and rustic — has a genuinely brilliant set of staircase ideas to draw from.

For a modern staircase, think clean lines, a limited colour palette (often white, black, grey, or warm neutrals), and statement art in simple frames or even unframed canvas. Floating shelves with sculptural objects, minimalist metal railings, and sleek pendant lighting all keep the space looking sharp and uncluttered.

A traditional staircase suits a more layered approach: stair runners in rich patterns, ornate balustrades, framed oil-style prints or botanical illustrations, and wall panelling with classic moulding. It's a style that rewards going a little bolder — deeper colours on the walls and heavier frames work brilliantly here.

Rustic staircases are my personal favourite to style. Think exposed wood banisters, distressed metal fixtures, woven wall hangings, and earthy tones. Mixing textures — rough linen, hammered iron, reclaimed timber — gives rustic staircases enormous warmth without any effort at all.

Quick Style Reference Guide

  • Modern: White or greige walls, unframed canvas or thin black frames, minimalist shelving, statement pendants
  • Traditional: Wall panelling, gallery frames in gold or dark wood, stair runners, botanical or portrait prints
  • Rustic: Exposed wood, macramé hangings, woven baskets on hooks, earthy terracotta tones, plants
  • Scandi/Japandi: Pale oak, pared-back prints, low-hung sconces, natural materials only
  • Industrial: Exposed brick, metal railings, monochrome photography, Edison-bulb pendants
Pro Tip: Before buying anything, hold paint swatches and art print samples against your staircase wall in both daytime and evening light. Stairwells can be much darker than you expect, and what looks perfect in a shop can look flat or dingy on the wall.

Wall Art and Gallery Wall Ideas for Staircases

A gallery wall on a staircase is one of those things that looks effortless when it's done well — but takes a bit of thought to get right. The key difference from a flat living room wall is that you're working with a diagonal space, so the composition needs to follow the angle of the stairs rather than sit as a neat horizontal block.

The most popular approach is what I call the "staircase stagger": a row of frames that steps upward with each tread, maintaining equal spacing between each piece. It reads as one unified display, but each frame sits at a different height. This works brilliantly with a mix of sizes — say, two or three larger anchor pieces surrounded by smaller prints and photographs.

I had a client in a Victorian terraced house in Bristol — she had a narrow staircase with high ceilings, and she'd bought about twelve small frames in different sizes but couldn't work out how to arrange them. We laid them out on the floor first (always do this), photographed it, then transferred the arrangement to the wall using paper templates before putting a single nail in. The result was stunning and took the guesswork out completely.

Gallery Wall Layout Options for Staircases

  • The Diagonal Stagger: Frames step upward in a diagonal line following the stair angle — the most classic choice
  • The Clustered Grid: A tight block of same-sized frames in a grid, works best on a landing or flat wall above stairs
  • The Eclectic Mix: Different sizes, frames, and even objects (mirrors, small shelves) arranged loosely — needs a consistent colour palette to hold it together
  • The Mono Gallery: All black-and-white photography in matching black frames — graphic, modern, and impossible to get wrong

Pro Tip: Use paper templates (cut to frame size) and low-tack masking tape to plan your gallery wall layout before you commit to any nails. Take a photo of the template arrangement on the wall — it's much easier to tweak on your phone than in real life.

How to Hang Art in a Stairwell — Step by Step

Knowing how to hang art in a stairwell is one of the most searched questions I come across, and honestly, it trips people up not because it's technically difficult, but because the angled wall messes with your spatial judgement. What looks level to your eye usually isn't, because the stairs themselves are on a slope.

The golden rule: hang art relative to the wall, not the floor. Use a spirit level every single time, and don't trust your eye alone in a stairwell — the angle of the stairs will fool you into hanging everything crooked.

When it comes to height, the standard guidance is to hang the centre of each artwork at roughly 145–150cm from the floor directly below that piece. In a stairwell, "the floor below" means the nearest tread, not the bottom of the stairs. This keeps everything proportional as you move up.

Step-by-Step Guide to Hanging Stairwell Art

  • Step 1: Decide on your layout. Lay all frames on the floor first and photograph your preferred arrangement.
  • Step 2: Cut paper templates the same size as each frame and tape them to the wall with low-tack tape.
  • Step 3: Step back (literally — go to the top or bottom of the stairs) and check the spacing looks even from a distance.
  • Step 4: Mark nail positions through each paper template using a pencil. Use a spirit level for every mark.
  • Step 5: Remove templates and hang the frames. Use picture hooks rated for the weight of each piece.
  • Step 6: Walk up and down the stairs slowly and check that nothing looks off from eye level in motion — this is the final test.
Pro Tip: On plasterboard staircase walls, always use wall anchors or find the stud when hanging heavier frames. Stairwells are high-traffic vibration zones — you don't want anything working loose over time.

How to Decorate a High Stairwell Wall

A high stairwell wall is simultaneously the most exciting and most intimidating canvas in any home. The sheer scale of it means that small art looks completely lost — and yet many people default to hanging a few small frames and wondering why the space still looks bare.

The honest answer to how to decorate a high stairwell wall is: go bigger than you think you need to. A single oversized print or canvas (think 100cm wide and taller) anchors the wall properly. Alternatively, a floor-to-ceiling arrangement of framed pieces — scaled up and spaced generously — works as a dramatic statement.

One approach I love for really tall stairwells is treating the wall like a mural backdrop. Large-format photographic prints, oversized botanical illustrations, or even peel-and-stick wallpaper murals can fill a tall stairwell beautifully without requiring scaffolding to hang.

Ideas for Tall Stairwell Walls

  • One oversized canvas or print as a single anchor statement
  • A floor-to-ceiling gallery arrangement with varied frame sizes
  • A large wallpaper mural panel behind the stair run
  • Oversized mirrors to bounce light and add depth
  • Wall-mounted sconces at two or three heights to draw the eye upward
  • Hanging macramé or textile art that fills vertical space naturally

Real Example: I worked with a family in a 1930s semi-detached who had a stunning tall stairwell but had covered it with eight tiny prints in mismatched frames. We replaced everything with two large-format prints and a single oversized mirror — the space looked three times the size within an afternoon.

How to Decorate an Enclosed Stairwell

Enclosed stairwells — the kind with walls on both sides and often no natural light — are tricky, but they're not hopeless. In fact, the enclosed nature of the space actually works in your favour: it creates a contained, immersive atmosphere that you can really lean into.

When I think about how to decorate an enclosed stairwell, the first thing I address is light. Without natural light, the space will feel oppressive unless you add artificial light at multiple points — wall-mounted sconces, LED strip lighting under handrails, or even a pendant that drops down the stairwell from above.

For enclosed staircase wall decorating ideas, light-reflective choices are your friends: pale paint colours, mirrors, metallic-framed art, and high-gloss or satin finishes on woodwork. I'd also suggest keeping the wall decor on one side only if the stairwell is narrow — both sides decorated in a tight space can feel claustrophobic.

Enclosed Stairwell Decor Checklist

  • Add wall-mounted sconces for warm, layered lighting
  • Use light paint colours — off-white, pale stone, or soft sage
  • Hang at least one mirror to maximise the sense of space
  • Keep wall decor on one wall only if the stairwell is under 90cm wide
  • Use a stair runner to add warmth underfoot without cluttering the walls
  • Add a single trailing plant on the landing above to draw the eye upward
Pro Tip: In an enclosed stairwell, a large mirror placed opposite the main light source will effectively double the perceived width of the space. This is the single quickest fix I know for a dark, cramped stairwell.

Staircase Railing and Balustrade Decorating Options

The railing and balustrade are structural elements, yes — but they're also a huge part of the visual character of your staircase. Updating them (or simply dressing them up) can make a bigger difference than anything you put on the walls.

If you have an older staircase with traditional timber spindles, painting them is one of the most cost-effective transformations available. Classic white or off-white spindles against a dark handrail looks crisp and timeless. For a more modern feel, painting spindles in a deep charcoal, navy, or even black gives a dramatic, high-end look at almost no cost.

Beyond paint, you can wrap newel posts in rope or leather for a nautical or rustic feel, add woven garlands for seasonal or permanent decorative interest, or swap outdated spindles for sleek glass panels or steel rods if your budget allows for a full update.

Option Best For Approximate Effort

Paint spindles dark (charcoal/black) Modern, industrial, Scandi homes Low — DIY weekend job

Replace with steel rod balusters Industrial or modern minimalist Medium — professional recommended
Wrap newel post in rope Rustic, coastal, Bohemian styles Low — DIY afternoon
Add woven/seasonal garland Any style for seasonal updates Very low — temporary
Pro Tip: Before you decide on new spindles or panels, check with a structural engineer or joiner that your existing newel posts can support the fixings. It's a quick check that saves expensive surprises later.

Lighting Ideas to Enhance Staircase Decor

Lighting is the most underused tool in staircase decorating — full stop. I genuinely believe you can have the most beautiful gallery wall in the world, but if your staircase is lit by a single harsh ceiling bulb, it will never look as good as it should.

The key principle is layered lighting. You want at least two sources in a staircase: ambient light (overall brightness for safety) and accent or decorative lighting that adds atmosphere. Wall-mounted sconces are the most popular choice because they sit at eye level, cast a warm glow, and add visual interest to the wall even when switched off.

LED strip lighting under the handrail or beneath each tread is a modern touch that looks brilliant at night and significantly improves stair safety. For tall stairwells, a pendant that drops down through the full height of the stairwell can be an extraordinary focal point — think an oversized drum shade or a sculptural cage pendant.

Staircase Lighting Options

  • Wall sconces: Best for adding warmth and visual interest at eye level
  • Under-tread LED strips: Modern, dramatic, and brilliant for safety
  • Pendant lights: Ideal for tall stairwells; choose scale carefully
  • Recessed ceiling spotlights: Clean and minimal; aim down the staircase run, not flat
  • Lantern-style pendants: Great for traditional or rustic staircases
  • Picture lights over key art pieces: For gallery walls — adds drama and draws the eye

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: Warm white bulbs (2700K–3000K) always look better in stairwells than cool white. Cool light makes the space feel clinical and tends to flatten wall colours — warm light makes everything feel considered and welcoming.

Colour Scheme and Paint Ideas Paired with Wall Decor

Choosing a colour scheme for your staircase is a bit different from choosing one for a room, because your staircase is usually a transitional space connecting different areas of the house. The colours need to feel cohesive with both your hallway and your upper landing — not just pretty in isolation.

My go-to approach is to pick one colour from your hall or landing and use the staircase as the place where you deepen or accent it. So if your hall is pale stone, your staircase wall might go in a warm taupe or even a deep heritage green — it creates a sense of progression as you move through the house.

Is painting your stairs a good idea? Absolutely, yes — painted stair risers (the vertical front face of each step) are one of the best budget updates you can do. Plain white risers make everything look cleaner and bigger, while painted risers in a contrasting colour add a playful, design-forward touch. Just make sure you use a durable floor or stair-specific paint and add a protective varnish over the top.

Staircase Colour Pairing Ideas

  • Pale stone + white woodwork: Safe, timeless, works in any home
  • Deep sage green + natural oak: Warm, organic, brilliant for Scandi or rustic styles
  • Charcoal or navy + white woodwork: Dramatic and confident — a strong statement
  • Blush pink + warm grey: Soft, modern, brilliant for a contemporary terraced house
  • Warm white + painted risers in a contrasting accent: Budget-friendly with big impact
Pro Tip: Always paint the staircase and landing the same colour on the ceiling and upper wall surfaces — it creates a visual flow that makes the space feel intentionally designed rather than just "decorated in sections".

Small vs Large Staircase Decorating Considerations

Not all staircases are created equal, and the approach that works for a dramatic Victorian double-height stairwell will feel completely wrong in a compact new-build. Getting the scale right is honestly the most important factor in staircase decorating.

In a small staircase, the biggest mistake people make is going too small with their art — using tiny frames that disappear against the wall. Counterintuitively, one medium-to-large print often looks better than five small ones in a tight space. It gives the eye somewhere clear to land without cluttering an already compact area.

In a large staircase, the challenge is filling the space without it feeling wallpapered or frantic. Breathing room between pieces matters. I always recommend that the gaps between frames should be at least as wide as the frame itself — this keeps the display feeling curated rather than crowded.

At a Glance: Small vs Large Staircase Decor Rules

Factor Small Staircase Large Staircase
Art size One medium statement piece Large anchors + supporting pieces
Number of pieces 1–3 maximum 5–12+ in a gallery arrangement
Colour palette Light and cohesive to open space Can handle bolder, deeper tones
Mirrors Essential — adds depth Optional accent piece
Lighting One sconce, keep it simple Layer multiple sources; pendant works well
Pro Tip: In a small staircase, choose frames with thin profiles (under 2cm wide) or go frameless. Heavy ornate frames make a small wall feel even smaller and can make the staircase feel cramped.

Shoppable Wall Art Recommendations Specific to Staircase Proportions

One of the gaps I notice in most staircase decorating guides is that they show you lovely inspiration images but never tell you what to actually buy. So here's my practical breakdown of the types of wall art that work best for staircase proportions — and why.

For a tall stairwell, you want prints or canvases in portrait orientation — taller than they are wide — which naturally echo the upward movement of the stairs. Abstract line art, tall botanical prints, and architectural photography in portrait format all look exceptional.

For a gallery wall arrangement stepping up with the stairs, mixing landscape and portrait prints in cohesive tones (black and white, or a limited earthy palette) gives the display visual rhythm without chaos. Matching frame colours — all black, all white, or all natural wood — ties mismatched print styles together instantly.

Wall Art Types for Staircase Proportions

  • Tall portrait prints (60x90cm or larger): Perfect for tall stairwells, echoes the upward movement
  • Square prints (50x50cm or 60x60cm): Great for creating uniform grid arrangements on a landing wall
  • Panoramic/wide landscape prints: Works well above a half-landing or on a large flat wall at the top of stairs
  • Abstract line art: Versatile, pairs with any interior style, never dates
  • Botanical or nature prints: Add organic warmth — particularly good in rustic or Scandi staircases
  • Black and white photography: Timeless and cohesive — the safest gallery wall choice

Pro Tip: When buying art for a staircase gallery, order all your prints at the same time and frame them before you hang anything. Seeing all the pieces together in your hand, in their frames, before anything goes on the wall, prevents the most common mistake: a mix of tones and depths that doesn't hang together.

Budget-Friendly vs Luxury Staircase Decorating Ideas

I work with clients at every budget level, and I genuinely believe you can achieve a beautiful staircase without spending a fortune — but you do need to be strategic about where you spend and where you save. The worst approach is to splash out on lots of small things that don't add up to anything cohesive.

At the budget end, painting is always your biggest bang for your buck. A fresh coat on the walls and woodwork, painted stair risers, and a printed geometric stair runner transforms a staircase for a fraction of the cost of a renovation. Add a couple of well-chosen prints in simple frames and a mirror, and you're done.

At the luxury end, the staircase is where bespoke really pays off. Custom joinery for the balustrade, a hand-tufted stair runner, original artwork or photography, and designer pendant lighting create a space that's genuinely one of a kind.

Budget vs Luxury: Where to Spend and Where to Save

Element Budget Option Luxury Option
Wall art Art prints in simple frames Original artworks or large-format prints in bespoke frames
Stair covering Painted risers + adhesive runner Hand-tufted or wool stair runner, professionally fitted
Balustrade Paint existing spindles Replace with glass panels or bespoke steel rods
Lighting Simple sconces, LED strips Designer pendants, integrated step lighting
Shelving Simple floating shelves Bespoke alcove shelving with integrated lighting

When clients ask how to modernise a staircase on a budget, my honest answer is always: start with paint, add one statement mirror, and choose two or three quality prints in matching frames. That combination alone will transform almost any staircase without you spending more than a couple of hundred pounds.

Pro Tip: Quality frames make budget prints look expensive. A simple print in a thick-profile black or natural oak frame looks like a deliberate, considered choice. The same print in a flimsy thin frame looks like an afterthought.

Common Staircase Decorating Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

After more than a decade of staircase consultations, I could write an entire book on the mistakes I see repeatedly. But I'll give you the most important ones here, because avoiding them is genuinely more valuable than any inspiration board.

The number one mistake is hanging art too low. People instinctively hang things at room-height — around 145cm from the floor — but on a staircase, that often means art ends up at knee level as you walk up. Always hang relative to the wall, following the stair angle, and aim to have the centre of each piece at eye level as you pass it on the stairs, not from the bottom of the staircase.

The second biggest mistake is a mismatch of frame styles with no unifying element. I visited a home where the client had bought frames over several years — gold, silver, black, white, and ornate wooden — all on the same wall. No single piece looked wrong individually, but together it was visual chaos. Picking one frame finish for a gallery wall is the single easiest fix.

What should not be done on a staircase? Cluttering the floor or treads with decorative objects. It's a safety hazard and it makes even a beautifully decorated staircase look messy. Keep the floor of your stairs completely clear — the walls and railing are where the decor lives.

Top Staircase Decorating Mistakes to Avoid

  • Hanging art too low — always follow the stair angle and eye-level rule
  • Mixing too many frame finishes with no unifying element
  • Placing objects on stair treads — a safety risk and a styling mistake
  • Choosing art that is too small for the wall — go bigger than you think
  • Ignoring lighting — a beautiful gallery wall in bad light always disappoints
  • Using too many colours in art and decor — a cohesive palette is key
  • Forgetting to account for the visual experience from both directions (going up and coming down)
Real Example: A client once showed me a staircase she'd decorated herself — lovely prints, good frames — but everything was hung in a perfectly level horizontal row. On a staircase, that horizontal line fought against the diagonal of the stairs and the whole display looked oddly tilted. We re-hung everything following the stair angle in an afternoon and the difference was immediate.

Staircase Wall Decor Ideas: Modern Takes Worth Trying

When I think about staircase wall decor ideas for a modern home, I immediately think about what the latest staircase trends are pointing toward — and right now, it's a move away from fussy gallery walls toward bolder, more intentional statements.

Modern stairwell wall art ideas tend to feature large-scale abstract art, oversized monochrome photography, or even a single dramatic sculptural piece rather than a collection. The idea is "less, but better" — fewer pieces, more considered, with generous space around each one.

Staircase wall decor ideas in a modern style also include architectural elements: wall panelling in a modern reeded or fluted profile, polished plaster finishes, or a graphic accent wall in a single bold colour. These work beautifully as a backdrop to a single piece of statement art or a large mirror.

Modern Staircase Wall Ideas to Try Now

  • One oversized abstract or monochrome print as the sole wall feature
  • Reeded or fluted MDF wall panelling for an architectural texture
  • Polished plaster in a warm tone — zero art needed, the wall is the feature
  • A large round mirror as a dramatic single accent
  • Wall-mounted sculptural lighting that doubles as an art piece
  • A single oversized macramé or woven textile piece for Boho-modern style

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: Modern staircase wall decor works best when you commit to restraint. If you're tempted to add "just one more thing", that is usually a sign to stop. The space between pieces is as important as the pieces themselves.

Staircase Decor Styles Worth Exploring

I find that staircase decorating trends evolve more slowly than other rooms — which is actually a good thing. You're making decisions that live with you for years, so it's worth looking at what genuinely suits your house rather than chasing trends. That said, here are the styles I'm most excited about right now that I think have genuine staying power.

The warm Japandi look — a blend of Japanese minimalism and Scandinavian cosiness — is producing some of the most beautiful staircase interiors I've seen. Pale oak treads, warm white walls, a single trailing plant, a ceramic vase on a floating shelf, and no art at all — just clean, calm intention.

At the opposite end, maximalist gallery walls are having a real moment in period homes. Floor-to-ceiling art arrangements in ornate frames, mixed with mirrors and decorative plates, feel genuinely theatrical and exciting. If your home has the bones for it, lean in.

Visual Inspiration

Explore complementary design ideas on our Home Decor by Trend page:

  • Modern Contemporary Home Decor Trend - sleek stylish staircase design ideas
  • Modern Glam Luxe Interior Trend - glamorous statement staircase decor inspiration
  • Cosy Minimalism Home Decor Trend - simple elegant staircase styling touches

More About Staircase Decorating — Expert Guidance Worth Reading

Getting the most from your staircase starts with understanding the space as a whole rather than decorating it in isolated elements.

The best staircase decorating is always joined up: the colour on the walls, the finish on the balustrade, the choice of lighting, and the art all work together as one composition. For a broader look at the full range of stair decorating possibilities — from open-riser treads to under-stair storage and mural-scale wallpaper — I always recommend reading around the topic. Stair decorating ideas - Grand Designs Magazine offers a fantastic overview of the wider possibilities and is well worth exploring if you want to push further beyond the walls.

What I'd add from my own experience is this: the staircase is worth investing in both time and thought, because it's genuinely one of the most used spaces in any home. You pass through it multiple times a day, every day. When it looks and feels right, it lifts your mood every single time you use it — and that's not a small thing.

WATCH: 27 Awesome Staircase Decorating Ideas

Ready to Transform Your Staircase? Here's Where to Start

If you've made it this far, you're probably already picturing what your staircase could look like — and that's the most important first step. The best thing about staircase decorating is that it doesn't need to happen all at once. Start with one decision: a colour, a piece of art, or a lighting upgrade. Build from there.

Whatever your budget, your style, or the size of your staircase, the core idea is the same: treat it as a real room rather than a corridor you happen to have to walk through. It deserves the same thought and care as any other space in your home — probably more, given how often you're in it.

And honestly? The staircase is often the space that surprises people most once they finally give it attention. Clients who were dreading the project almost always end up saying it became their favourite part of the house.

So tell me — what's the biggest challenge with your staircase right now? Is it the height, the lack of light, knowing where to even start with art? I'd love to hear what you're working with.

small games room ideas.bodyHtml:
Small games room ideas don't have to mean compromise. With the right layout, clever storage, and some seriously well-chosen wall art and decor, even the tiniest spare room can become a space you're genuinely proud of — whether you're into console gaming, board games, or hosting a noisy games night with friends.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever looked at a small room and thought, "there's absolutely no way I can turn this into a games room"? I've been there — and so have dozens of clients I've worked with over the years. The good news is that the right wall art choices alone can completely transform how big, how atmospheric, and how "finished" a small games room feels.

Quick answer: The best small games room ideas combine smart space-saving furniture and storage with strategic wall art, lighting, and colour choices that visually expand the room. Focus on vertical space, multi-use pieces, and decor that reflects the room's purpose — whether that's a chill adult gaming den or a fun-packed kids' games room.

A games room is simply a dedicated space in your home set aside for play — whether that means video games, board games, table tennis, or card nights. It doesn't need to be large to work brilliantly. With unique wall art and carefully chosen unique home decor, even a box room can feel purposeful, atmospheric, and genuinely inviting. This guide covers everything from layout and storage to colour psychology, murals, DIY decor ideas, and the mistakes that make small spaces feel even smaller.

  • Small Game Room Ideas for Adults, Kids and Rooms with a Bed
